Thanks Samantha — great framing and very reasonable asks. Quick read: yes, we can do a 3-year prepay that preserves list pricing and offers a structured annual reconciliation.

Quick thoughts we can put into a term sheet:
- Base: 3-year prepay equal to 12 months of your current expected consumption at current list rate (Tier A).
- Discount schedule: 18% off list for the 3-year commit, with an incremental 2% uplift (to 20%) if you sign within 30 days.
- Usage swing: annual +/-20% band. If actuals fall below 80% of forecast, you receive a credit equal to the difference priced at the contracted (post-discount) rate, carried as a rollover credit to the next year. If actuals exceed 120%, you draw from the prepay balance at the contracted rate.
- Escrow/creditline: we can allocate up to 10% of the prepay into a redeemable credit pool for burst usage. Unused portion after year 3 is refundable or can convert to a renewal credit.
- True-up: annual reconciliation with a 45-day settlement window; negative balances move forward as credits, positives reduce remaining prepay.
- Termination: standard limited termination rights; escrow conversion rules outlined in term sheet.

I'll draft the term schedule and attach a worked example showing year-by-year cash flows and credits. Vivek — can you confirm finance is comfortable with the rollover credit being treated as a liability that offsets invoicing? Marissa — can you prepare the worked example spreadsheet?

Sincerely,
Olga Petrov

Confirmed — finance okay with treating rollover credits as deferred revenue reduction (i.e., liability offset) provided we meet simple controls:
- Credits expire after the 3-year term unless converted to a renewal credit by mutual consent.
- There is a clear monthly consumption ledger we maintain (we can push a CSV monthly).
- Escrow pool is a contractual earmark of the prepay balance — refundable if unused after year 3.

Two cautions:
1) We should cap cumulative negative reconciliation exposure to 40% of the original prepay in any single year (protect Redwood from extremely low usage).
2) Legal must keep a short clause that prevents gaming of the escrow pool (e.g., circular transfers).
